Minimum wage should be just enough to support yourself, and not a four-person family. If you are at the stage where you have a family, you should be earning more than minimum wage. Minimum wage is for starting out. You should not be working for it your whole life.
Which brings up the issues of outsourcing and cheap consumer goods. There is a big pile of issues behind the living wage arguments, it is hard to discuss this topic without it getting complicated.

With a federal living wage, people who are in the lower income brackets will now have the resources to support themselves. This increase in income allows those people to afford the housing, clothing, and food that most of us would consider necessary. Since this income bracket isn't making enough extra money to horde cash or invest outside of the local economy, that income gets pushed back into the community. Even the simple act of opening a bank account (Something which people living paycheck to paycheck might not be able to do) helps to inject funds into the economy. This raises the floor for everyone, and pushes our idea of what a minimum standard of living should be.

This would also have the benefit of getting a number of individuals out of the public assistance programs that many of them currently need to be on in order to afford basic housing and groceries. When companies don't provide a living wage to their workers, we end up subsidizing them through the taxes we pay to keep these programs funded. I'm not saying these programs shouldn't exist, but they shouldn't be responsible for subsidizing the payroll of corporations.

The downside is that companies will need to offset this cost by raising prices on the products they sell or find a way to outsource their labor. This may mean that there will be fewer jobs available for those people who are only qualified for minimum wage jobs which may lead to higher unemployment. Because unemployment benefits only last for a given amount of time (as apposed to public assistance for low income earners) we may end up with a sizable group of people that are unemployable and have no income. However, giving low income earners more money might create new revenue streams which would increase hiring.

I think the biggest con is that we really have no idea exactly how this would effect everything. While the perceived benefits are great, the possible downsides could be devastating to a large number of people who are directly effected. No one wants the be the person responsible for negative effects that could arise if things go wrong.

I think that unless we make sweeping changes to the economy as a whole a living minimum wage isn't a real possibility. The fact of the matter is jobs like McDonalds, Wal-Mart and other low skill jobs aren't meant to be long term, supporting jobs unless you move into management positions. It comes down to supply and demand. The fact is that low/no-skill workers are available in droves and there aren't as many positions as workers, so high supply and low demand. This only deepens with illegal immigrants flooding into the country adding more workers to the low/no-skill pool, and many of which who are willing to work for less. The simple truth is that if you want to make a living wage you need a skill or education that puts you at a higher demand.

We have raised the minimum wage several times, and the workers are still in the same situation because all it does is cause the economy to re-balance itself putting them back in the same situation, just with bigger numbers that now mean less. Now companies are showing what they will do if the wage goes up, for instance McDonalds will put in terminals to take over the place of employees who take orders, so thats probably 4-8 jobs per store gone at 14,267 stores, thats 57,068-114,136 people who now have no wage because they have been replaced by a machine.

TL:DR increasing minimum wage is like a band-aide on a bullet wound, its effects are short lived and will never do what you want.
